what: An AI agent is an LLM running in a loop: it picks the next step, calls a tool, reads the result and repeats until the task is done or a limit is reached.
like: Like a new intern with a phone and a checklist: try something, see what happened, try the next thing, and check with you before spending money.
why: Handles open-ended tasks where you can't script the steps in advance
Works with real systems through tools, so each step is checked against real results
One model plus many tools (often via MCP) covers search, code, files and APIs

nodes.t: Human approval|yes or no on risky steps

steps.d: A person or another system hands over a task, the tools the agent may use, and limits such as a maximum number of steps.
The loop sends the goal, history and tool list to the LLM. The model either answers, or asks for a tool by name with JSON arguments that match its schema.
Your code runs the call: a local function, a tool on an MCP server via tools/call, or code inside a sandbox. The model only asks; your code does the work.
Before deleting, paying or sending, the loop asks a human for a yes or no. The MCP spec says a person should always be able to deny a tool call.
The tool result goes back into the context as ground truth. The loop repeats while the model asks for tools, and stops on a final answer or at the step limit.
Facts worth keeping go to a long-term memory store for later sessions. Every model call and tool call is recorded as a trace, so you can debug and run evals.

numbers.l: standard MCP transports: stdio (local) and Streamable HTTP (remote)
each MCP client inside the host talks to exactly one server

strict (schema-checked) tools allowed per Claude request

choices.d: If you know the steps, write them as a workflow in code: cheaper and predictable. Use an agent only when the model must decide the path itself.
Cap turns (for example max_turns) and total tokens or time per task. When the cap is hit, stop cleanly and report progress instead of looping.
Few, clear tools with good descriptions and strict schemas. Shape arguments so mistakes are hard (poka-yoke), and return helpful error text the model can fix from.
Reads run freely; writes that cost money, delete data or contact people wait for a human yes. Show the exact tool inputs in the request.
Short-term memory is the context window; summarise or compact it as it grows. Keep durable facts in a long-term store the agent reads at the start.

instead.why: One clear step? A single LLM call is cheaper and faster
A fixed tool call in your code, with no open-ended loop
Big jobs split across specialist agents under a lead
Answering from documents usually needs retrieval, not autonomy

breaks.d: The agent repeats the same search or edit and never finishes.
breaks.see: Turn count near the limit, the same tool call again and again in traces
breaks.fix: A step limit, a check for repeated calls, clearer success criteria in the prompt

breaks.d: Vague tool descriptions lead to the wrong call or invalid inputs.
breaks.see: Tool errors (isError true) and retries in traces
breaks.fix: Better names and docs, strict schemas, error messages that say how to fix the input

breaks.d: Long tasks pile tool results into the context window.
breaks.see: Rising input tokens per turn, slower and costlier steps, early stops
breaks.fix: Clear old tool results, compact the history, keep key facts in a memory store

breaks.d: A web page or file the agent reads contains text that tries to steer it (prompt injection).
breaks.see: Unexpected tool calls right after reading outside content
breaks.fix: Treat tool output as data, least-privilege tools, a sandbox, human approval for risky actions

breaks.d: Each step is a little uncertain, so long runs drift and cost more.
breaks.see: Eval pass rate falls as tasks get longer; cost per task climbs
breaks.fix: Shorter loops, checkpoints with a human, evals on full runs, a workflow where steps are known

say: I'll start with a workflow and only make it an agent where the path truly depends on what the model finds.
The agent loop calls the LLM with the tool list, runs any tool it asks for, feeds the result back, and stops on a final answer or a max-turns limit.
Tools come from MCP servers so they are reusable, and anything that writes, pays or sends goes through a human approval step; code runs in a sandbox.
Every run is traced, model calls and tool calls as spans, and I keep an eval set of real tasks to check success rate, steps and cost before each change.

followups.q: Workflow or agent - how do you choose?
followups.a: If the steps are known, a workflow in code is cheaper, faster and easier to test. Use an agent when the number and order of steps depend on what it discovers, like debugging or research. Agents trade cost and latency for flexibility.

followups.q: How does the agent remember things?
followups.a: Short-term memory is the context window: the conversation and tool results. Long-term memory is an outside store (files, a database or vectors) the agent reads and writes through tools, so knowledge survives across sessions.

followups.q: What is MCP and why use it?
followups.a: The Model Context Protocol is an open standard, built on JSON-RPC, for connecting AI apps to tools and data. A server exposes tools, resources and prompts once, and any MCP host can use them.

followups.q: How do you test an agent?
followups.a: Build an eval set of real tasks with clear pass checks, run the full loop in a sandbox, and read the traces. Track success rate, steps, tokens and cost per task, and rerun the set on every prompt or tool change.

today: In December 2025 Anthropic gave MCP to the new Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation, co-founded with Block and OpenAI, so the protocol is now run as a shared open standard.

check.q: When should an agent stop its loop?
check.a: On a final answer, or when it hits the step or budget limit
d: Only when the user closes the app
Whenever a tool returns an error
check.why: A final answer ends the loop; a max-turns cap keeps it in control. Tool errors are fed back so the model can fix its call.

check.q: The agent is about to delete a customer's data. What should happen?
check.a: Pause and ask a human to approve or deny
d: Run it right away to save time
Ask the LLM if it is sure
Retry it twice to be safe
check.why: Risky, hard-to-undo actions go through human approval. MCP says a person should be able to deny tool calls.

check.q: In MCP, what does a server expose?
check.why: Servers offer focused capabilities. By design they don't see the whole conversation; the host keeps that.

check.q: The steps of a task are always the same. What fits best?
check.a: A workflow in code that calls the LLM at fixed points
d: An agent with no step limit
check.why: Known steps make a workflow cheaper, faster and easier to test than an agent.
